newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean to develop planes with Europe's AIR.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean to develop planes with Europe's AIR.

text.p: After failing twice in the past year to secure an aerospace partner, South Korea on Friday signed a memorandum of understanding with a European consortium to jointly develop medium-sized passenger jets.

The South Korean government and company officials applauded the deal, but analysts warned the final structure of the partnership could hamper South Korea's goal of becoming a regional and global planemaking power.
"The local aircraft industry so far has been confined to serving foreign planemakers as parts subcontractors," said a senior official at the trade ministry's aerospace industry department.
"This deal will provide important opportunities for us to acquire valuable technology and experience," he said.
The memorandum is valid for six months, but the parties agreed verbally to settle details of the partnership within three months, according to a trade ministry statement.

Under the memorandum, the Korean Commercial Aircraft Development Consortium agreed to take a minimum 30 percent stake in a $1.2 billion project by Aero International Regional (AIR) to make passenger jets with 58 to 84 seats, the ministry statement said.
AIR expects annual sales of about 50 units, valued at $20 million to $22 million each, over 20 years beginning in 2001, the statement said.
South Korea's 14-member consortium is led by Samsung Aerospace Industries Co and includes Korean Air Lines Co, Daewoo Heavy Industries Co and Hyundai Space and Aircraft Co.
AIR is equally owned by France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc and Italy's Alenia.
But unless South Korea is allowed to establish assembly lines on its own soil, its goal of joining the exclusive club of world-class integrated aircraft makers might never be realised, analysts said.
"As long as AIR retains the initiative, South Korea's role will likely be limited," said Ann Young-su, fellow at the Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade.
China's efforts to promote its own project to make 100-seat passenger jets has also raised doubts about South Korea's potential to profitably market its planes in the region.
Talks between Seoul and Beijing to establish a joint venture to make planes with technology from a third country fell apart last June over a dispute over the location of the assembly line.

"Even if South Korea is given the right to oversee marketing in Asia, I have doubts about the profitability in regional markets minus China," said Sonia Song, an analyst at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.

The memorandum stipulates that airplane assembly will initially be done by AIR or its member companies, while South Korea will be in charge of aircraft completion work and delivery to Asian customers, the trade ministry official said.

A bid by Samsung Aerospace, which later invited other members of the domestic consortium, to take over the bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker broke down at the end of last year, largely because of a disagreement over the terms, including the purchase price.
